About: Centrifugal Force — A Ball on a Merry-Go-Round (3D)

Source

Lecture
Classical mechanics — non-inertial frames & fictitious forces (rotating-frame case; the linearly accelerating frame's −ma pseudo force is not covered here)
Simulation
"The Centrifugal Force — A Ball on a Merry-Go-Round" · 3D carousel with two synchronized views (ground/inertial ↔ rotating camera, plus side-by-side), trails in both frames, radial-fling prediction confronted in the guided inquiry
Concept
The centrifugal force is not a real interaction: it appears only when motion is described in a rotating frame (Fcf = mω²r, radially outward); the ground view shows straight-line or at-rest motion under real forces only.
Serves
Frame-dependence of fictitious forces · Newton's 1st law as the ground-frame explanation · reading and scaling F = mω²r (m = 1 kg, ω = 1.5 rad/s, r = 2 m → 4.5 N outward; ω = 1, r = 1 → 1 N; F ∝ ω² and ∝ r)
Inquiry
Where is the outward force in the ground view? · How does Fcf change when ω doubles? · Which facts are identical in both frames?
Misconception
"Centrifugal force is a real outward interaction acting on the ball." Nothing exerts it; the released ball's ground-frame path is a straight tangent line, never a radial fling — the outward push exists only in the rotating description.

Centrifugal Force: Merry-Go-Round
drag to orbit, scroll to zoom

Guided Inquiry

1 · Feel the “push”

Camera on Rotating. A backstop holds the ball at r = 2.0 m. Press Release ball when you want it to let go. Watch the violet arrow — Fcf = mω²r — and how the ball drifts outward as if shoved. Its Fcent readout grows as r grows (Fcf ∝ r; the drawn arrow caps at a maximum length for readability).

2 · Predict — the ground path

Same release, now imagined from the Ground (inertial) camera. After the backstop lets go, what path does the ball take?

3 · Hunt for the pusher

Camera on Ground. After release, which horizontal force arrows remain? None. The cyan trail is a straight tangent at v = ωr. Gravity ↓ and the normal ↑ cancel — Newton’s 1st law.

4 · Scale the ghost force

ω is now 2.00 rad/s at the same r = 2.0 m. Read the badge: Fcf = 8.00 N (was 4.50 N at 1.50 rad/s; at ω = 1 → 2.00 N). Double ω ⇒ ×4 force, because Fcf = mω²r ∝ ω².

5 · Both cameras

Open Both cameras and press Release ball. The cyan ground trail is a straight tangent; the orange rotating trail is the same motion re-described on the carousel. No radial “fling.”

6 · Frame-proof vs frame-only

Events (release, rim crossing) and every real force are the same in both cameras. Centrifugal (and Coriolis) appear only in the rotating description — no object exerts them, no reaction partner. That is the fingerprint of a fictitious force — what JEE problems call a pseudo force.

01

At a glance

A ball is held by a backstop on a spinning carousel, and you choose when to let it go. The sim shows the same motion from a camera on the ground and from a camera turning with the carousel.

What you'll learn

  • How one motion looks different from a ground camera and from a rotating camera.
  • How the centrifugal force F = mω²r depends on ω and on r.
  • Which forces are real and which appear only in one view.
  • What "pseudo force" means in JEE problems.
The ball sits a distance r from the axis. The backstop keeps it there until you release it.

What's on screen

  • 3D stage: the carousel, the ball and the backstop. Drag to orbit, scroll to zoom.
  • Cyan trail in the ground view and orange trail in the rotating view: the ball's path in that view.
  • Green arrow N: the backstop's push, a real force. Violet arrow Fcent: in the rotating view only.
  • Centrifugal force readout: Fcent = mω²r in newtons.
See itWatch the held ball from the ground camera. Watch for: the ball going round with the carousel and the green N (backstop) arrow pointing inward.

Fixed: ball mass m = 1 kg, carousel radius 3.4 m, frictionless deck and floor. The ball disappears 9.55 m from the axis.

03

From the carousel, a held ball feels an outward push

On the carousel the held ball is at rest. The backstop pushes it inward with a real force N, so something outward must balance N. In the rotating view that outward term is the centrifugal force:

Fcent = mω²r, directed outward
m is the ball's mass, ω the carousel's angular speed and r the ball's distance from the axis.

While the ball is held, N = mω²r as well. With m = 1 kg, ω = 1.50 rad/s and r = 2.0 m, both are 4.50 N. After release the sim recomputes mω²r at the ball's current distance, so the violet arrow's label changes as the ball moves.

See itSwitch to the Rotating camera. Watch for: the violet arrow labelled Fcent = 4.50 N pointing outward, and the green N arrow pointing inward.
04

From the ground, a released ball goes straight

After release, no horizontal force acts on the ball, because the deck and the floor are frictionless. Gravity and the normal force cancel. By Newton's first law its velocity stays constant, so it moves along a straight tangent at the speed it already had:

v = ωr

At ω = 1.50 rad/s and r = 2.0 m, v = 3.00 m/s. The ball reaches the carousel's edge, 3.4 m from the axis, after sliding 2.75 m in 0.92 s, and then keeps the same speed on the floor.

Before release the backstop supplied the inward force that bent the path into a circle. Nothing supplies it afterwards.

See itRelease the ball with the Ground camera. Watch for: a straight cyan trail leaving the release point along the tangent.
05

Centrifugal force grows as ω² and as r

Since Fcent = mω²r, doubling ω multiplies the force by 4, and doubling r multiplies it by 2. At r = 2.0 m:

ω1.00 rad/s1.50 rad/s2.00 rad/s
Fcent2.00 N4.50 N8.00 N

At ω = 1.50 rad/s, r = 1.0 m gives 2.25 N and r = 3.0 m gives 6.75 N. The violet arrow's length is capped so that it fits on screen, so read the number, not the length.

See itSet ω = 2.00 rad/s in the Rotating camera. Watch for: the violet arrow labelled Fcent = 8.00 N, against 4.50 N at ω = 1.50 rad/s.
06

The two cameras describe one motion

The orange path is the cyan straight line re-described in coordinates that turn with the carousel. At release the ball is at rest relative to the carousel, because v = ωr is exactly the speed of the deck beneath it. It then drifts outward and falls behind the spin.

With ω = 1.50 rad/s and r = 2.0 m, the ball is 24.8° behind its release radius by the time it reaches the carousel's edge.

For this curve to obey F = ma in the rotating view, two terms are added to the real forces, which are zero here:

ma′ = Freal + mω²r r̂ − 2mΩ × v′
The last term is the Coriolis term. The centrifugal term acts along the radius, and the Coriolis term bends the path sideways.
See itOpen Both cameras and release the ball. Watch for: a straight cyan trail on the left, and on the right the ball drifting off the carousel with an orange trail.
07

Pseudo forces have no source

Events and real forces are the same in both views. The ball is released at the same moment and place, and the backstop's push N appears in both.

The centrifugal and Coriolis terms appear only in the rotating view. No object exerts them, and they have no reaction partner. Forces of this kind, which exist only because the frame accelerates, are called pseudo or fictitious forces.

A JEE problem asks for one when it says "in the frame of the carousel". Add the pseudo force to the real forces, then use F = ma in that frame.

See itOpen Both cameras with the ball held. Watch for: the green N (backstop) arrow in both views, and the violet arrow in the rotating view only.
08

Where it matters

  • Turning vehicles. In a car turning left, you seem pushed to the right. From the road, your body is trying to go straight, and the door and the seat push you inward.
  • Centrifuges. In the lab frame the tube wall supplies the inward force that turns the sample. In the rotor's frame the same sample is pressed outward with mω²r.
  • Linear pseudo forces. A frame with acceleration a needs a pseudo force −ma on every mass. This sim covers the rotating case only.
Go deeper

The sim shows the Coriolis term only after you switch it on in the rotating view. For a ball at rest in the rotating frame it is zero, because it is proportional to v′. That is why the ball leaves the carousel along the radius in the rotating view and only then curves.

09

Summary

In one line. The sim releases one ball from a spinning carousel and shows the motion twice, from a ground camera and from a rotating camera.

Key points

  • Fcent = mω²r points outward and exists only in the rotating view.
  • From the ground, the released ball goes straight along the tangent at v = ωr.
  • The two paths are one motion described in two frames.

Common mix-ups

  • "The spin flings the ball straight out along the spoke." After release nothing pushes it. It keeps its tangential velocity.
  • "Centrifugal force is a real force on the ball." It is a pseudo force. No object exerts it.
  • "The backstop's force is fictitious too." N is real, and both cameras show it.

Things to try on your own

  • Release at r = 1.0 m and at r = 3.0 m with the Ground camera, and compare the speeds with v = ωr.
  • Set ω = 0.50 rad/s and read Fcent, then predict the value at ω = 1.00 rad/s.
  • In the Rotating camera, switch on the Coriolis arrow and release the ball.
